items.stem: A checkout agent runs six scoped tools at a 0.4% misroute rate across 90,000 monthly requests. Product wants twelve general-purpose tools added "for flexibility," though logs show no request needs a capability outside the six. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Add the twelve tools, but restrict their availability to business hours to limit exposure.
Add one narrowly scoped tool for the cross-role lookup the logs show is missing.
Add the twelve tools and log every invocation so unnecessary use can be reviewed later.
Decline the addition; the six-tool surface already meets the workflow at no added token cost.

items.whyRight: The six scoped tools already cover every logged request pattern, so the requirement is already satisfied. Adding twelve general-purpose tools for unmeasured future flexibility pays a token cost on every request and reintroduces confusable neighbours without fixing anything the current metrics show is broken.

whyWrong.A: Restricting the new tools to business hours narrows a time window, not the tool count; the token cost and confusable-neighbour risk persist for every request the rest of the day.
whyWrong.B: The stem's own logs already show no request needs a capability the current six don't cover, so there is no missing cross-role lookup to build a tool for.
whyWrong.C: Logging invocations records unnecessary use after it already happened; it never prevents the token cost or the misroute risk the extra tools would add.

items.t1Clause: logs show no request needs a capability outside the six
items.factAnswerRaw: Decline the addition; the six-tool surface already meets the workflow at no added token cost.

items.stem: A reimbursement agent's daily approval capability needs provable audit logging under a new compliance mandate; its delete capability is never invoked. The team proposes a system-prompt line telling the agent to record its own actions. What should the architect implement instead?

opts.t: Remove the prompt-level logging instruction and rely on the model to self-police the delete capability.
Replace the prompt line with a more detailed, carefully worded self-reporting instruction for every action.
Remove the delete capability from the tool configuration, and log every approval call at the tool-invocation layer.
Keep both capabilities, and log every approval and delete call at the tool-invocation layer.

items.whyRight: The compliance requirement is proof of action, which a prompt instruction cannot guarantee since the model can omit or misreport it. Enforcing the log at the tool-invocation layer makes it deterministic, and removing the never-used delete capability closes the actual privilege gap.

whyWrong.A: Dropping the logging instruction abandons the proof-of-action requirement entirely, and self-policing does nothing about the delete capability still sitting unused in the configuration.
whyWrong.B: A more detailed instruction is still a prompt-level self-report the model can skip or misstate; the audit mandate needs proof, not better wording.
whyWrong.D: The scenario states the delete capability is never invoked; logging it does not close the actual gap, which is an unneeded privilege still sitting in the configuration.

items.t1Clause: its delete capability is never invoked
items.factAnswerRaw: Remove the delete capability from the tool configuration, and log every approval call at the tool-invocation layer.

items.stem: A risk-classification service faces a regulator-mandated p95 latency SLA of 2,000ms that cannot be relaxed, currently met with no slack. Compliance also wants a 6-point accuracy gain, but every available accuracy lever adds latency. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Add a self-critique pass for the full accuracy gain, and request a one-time exception to the regulator SLA.
Apply the cheapest accuracy-per-millisecond lever that fits the SLA, accept a smaller gain, and report the shortfall.
Switch to a larger generation model for the full gain, since the SLA has margin to absorb it.
Reduce retrieved chunks to free latency budget for a reranking stage that reaches the full gain.

items.whyRight: The SLA is regulator-mandated and cannot be relaxed, and no accuracy lever is free, so the only defensible move is the cheapest lever that stays inside the budget, taking a smaller accuracy gain and reporting the remaining shortfall honestly to the business.

whyWrong.A: The scenario states the SLA cannot be relaxed; requesting an exception discards the one constraint that is fixed to fully satisfy the one that is negotiable.
whyWrong.C: The stem states the SLA is already met with no slack; a larger model adds latency the budget does not have to absorb.
whyWrong.D: Cutting retrieved context removes something the workflow requires and usually loses more accuracy than a reranking stage would recover in this budget.

items.t1Clause: the SLA is regulator-mandated and cannot be relaxed
items.factAnswerRaw: Apply the cheapest accuracy-per-millisecond lever that fits the SLA, accept a smaller gain, and report the shortfall.

items.stem: A support request passes through an intake agent, a triage tool, and a specialist agent across 40,000 tickets a day, each logging under its own request ID. Diagnosing a wrong answer requires reconstructing the full path. What should the architect implement?

opts.t: Instrument tool calls and retrieved context at each hop, but keep each service's own separate request ID.
Propagate a single correlation ID from the intake agent through every downstream hop and tool call.
Add per-stage timing to each service's logs to see where the response spends time.
Have an engineer manually cross-reference timestamps across each service's logs to reconstruct the path.

items.whyRight: A request that crosses three separate services fragments into three disconnected logs unless one identifier ties every hop together. Propagating a single correlation ID from intake onward is the only option that lets engineers reassemble the full path a specific wrong answer actually took.

whyWrong.A: Richer per-hop instrumentation still leaves three separate request IDs; the trace still cannot be reassembled into one path across services.
whyWrong.C: Per-stage timing diagnoses a latency regression, not a correctness problem; it says nothing about which hop caused the wrong answer.
whyWrong.D: Manual timestamp cross-referencing reconstructs by hand, per incident, what a correlation ID would have made automatic and repeatable at 40,000 tickets a day.

items.t1Clause: diagnosing a wrong answer requires reconstructing the full path
items.factAnswerRaw: Propagate one correlation ID through every hop

items.stem: A stable RAG system's answer quality drops the same night a scheduled 40,000-document refresh completes with full re-index coverage and an unchanged chunking configuration. The refresh pipeline shows no errors. What should the architect investigate next?

opts.t: Re-run the refresh pipeline end to end, since the timing points to the ingestion job as the cause.
Lower the retrieval top-k so fewer, more targeted chunks reach the generation step.
Check whether the embedding model version changed in the same deployment window, independent of the refresh.
Add a manual review step where an analyst spot-checks degraded answers before they reach users.

items.whyRight: The refresh completed cleanly with full coverage and an unchanged chunking scheme, so it is a coincidence, not the cause. A version change to the embedding model in the same window would silently shift the vector space and degrade retrieval without any refresh-side error.

whyWrong.A: The stem already states the pipeline shows no errors and coverage is full; re-running it targets a cause the evidence has already ruled out.
whyWrong.B: Reducing top-k changes how many chunks reach generation, not which vector space they were matched against; it does not touch the actual cause.
whyWrong.D: Manual spot-checking catches degraded answers after users could see them; it diagnoses nothing about why retrieval degraded in the first place.

items.t1Clause: the refresh pipeline shows no errors
items.factAnswerRaw: Check whether the embedding model version changed in the same deployment window, independent of the refresh.

items.stem: Applying the principle that a present-but-poorly-ranked document calls for reranking rather than added depth, a support-search system's correct document sits at rank 11 of 20 candidates on 92% of matching queries. What should the architect implement?

opts.t: Raise top-k from 20 to 50 so the correct document is captured further down the list.
Replace the retrieval mechanism with a different embedding model to improve match quality.
Add a reranking stage that reorders the existing top-20 candidates before passing the top few into context.
Lower the generation temperature so the model weighs the top-ranked chunk more heavily.

items.whyRight: The correct document is already inside the candidate set on 92% of matching queries; the failure is ranking, not absence. Reordering the existing top-20 with a reranking stage fixes exactly that, without the added tokens and latency a wider retrieval pass would cost.

whyWrong.A: The document is already retrieved; widening top-k floods context with lower-relevance chunks and adds cost without fixing where rank 11 sits.
whyWrong.B: Swapping the embedding model replaces a mechanism that is already surfacing the correct document, to solve a ranking problem it does not cause.
whyWrong.D: Temperature governs token sampling during generation; it has no effect on which candidate document the retrieval step ranked eleventh.

items.t1Clause: the correct document sits at rank 11 of 20 candidates
items.factAnswerRaw: Add a reranking stage over the existing candidate set
